title: Consumer Groups: Distributed Load Balancing
description: Understand consumer groups, how they enable horizontal scaling, and the trade-offs between competing and shared consumers.

data.text: **Consumer groups** are a fundamental scaling mechanism in event-streaming platforms like Apache Kafka. When multiple consumers join the same consumer group, they split the partitions of a topic among themselves — each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in the group. This enables horizontal processing: you can add more consumers to handle higher throughput, and the broker automatically rebalances partition assignments.

When a consumer joins a group, it declares a `group.id`. The Kafka group coordinator assigns each consumer a subset of the topic's partitions. Within a group, consumers are **cooperative** — they do not duplicate work. However, consumers in **different** groups each receive a full copy of every message, making consumer groups the mechanism that distinguishes load-balanced processing from multi-consumer broadcasting.

data.text: Kafka's default `RangeAssignor` assigns partitions alphabetically, which can lead to uneven distribution when topics have uneven partition counts. The `RoundRobinAssignor` distributes partitions evenly across consumers regardless of topic. The `CooperativeStickyAssignor` minimizes partition movement during rebalances, reducing processing pauses.

data.text: Consumer groups implement the **competing consumers** pattern: multiple consumers share the work of processing messages from the same topic. This is distinct from having multiple consumers in different groups, where each group independently receives every message. Use competing consumers to increase throughput; use multiple groups when you need independent processing pipelines on the same event stream.

data.title: Consumers Cannot Exceed Partitions
data.text: A consumer group with more consumers than topic partitions leaves some consumers idle. To scale further, increase the number of partitions — but note that repartitioning a live topic requires careful planning to avoid key-ordering violations.

terms.definition: A named set of consumers that cooperatively process messages from a set of topic partitions. Each partition is consumed by only one group member.
An ordered, immutable sequence of messages within a Kafka topic. Partitions are the unit of parallelism and are distributed across consumer group members.
The process by which the Kafka group coordinator reassigns partitions to consumers when consumers join or leave the group.
A pattern where multiple consumers share the workload of a single queue or topic partition set, improving throughput and fault tolerance.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Consumer groups allow horizontal scaling by sharing partitions among consumers.
Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in the group.
Multiple consumer groups on the same topic receive full copies (fanout).
Adding more consumers than partitions results in idle consumers.

items.question: What happens during a consumer group rebalance?
items.answer: When a consumer joins or leaves the group, the group coordinator triggers a rebalance. All consumers pause consumption while partition assignments are recalculated. Modern brokers use incremental rebalancing (KIP-429) to minimize this pause, but some disruption is always expected.

items.question: Can a partition have multiple consumers in the same group?
items.answer: No. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within a consumer group. If you need parallel processing of a single partition's messages, you must use multiple consumer groups (each gets a full copy) or partition the data further.

items.question: How does this differ from RabbitMQ competing consumers?
items.answer: RabbitMQ uses a simple round-robin dispatch across consumers on a single queue. Kafka consumer groups use explicit partition assignment, which provides ordering guarantees (messages in a partition are processed in order by one consumer) and better scalability through partition-level parallelism.
